extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental science, and readers of philosophy/methodology of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using the classical four methods of induction (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and supporting operations (definition, deduction, experiment) to infer causal laws from empirical instances. Includes cautions about limits of induction, examples (poisons, induced electricity, dew), and how to combine methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify an antecedent common to all instances in which a phenomenon occurs; infer that the common antecedent is a cause (or one of the causes) of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when many diverse instances share only one common circumstance. Example: Liebig’s induction that metallic poisons cause death by forming insoluble compounds with animal tissues — in all observed instances the metallic compound is brought into contact with animal substance and the common result is conversion into a compound resisting putrefaction. Anti-pattern: do not infer causation if other unrecognized common factors might exist; use with other methods to strengthen certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare otherwise similar instances where the effect is present and where it is absent; if they differ only by one antecedent, that antecedent is the cause (or absence of it explains absence of effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires ideally a positive and negative instance differing in only one circumstance. Examples: antidotes to arsenious acid (hydrated peroxide of iron) demonstrating that preventing formation of the insoluble compound prevents poisoning. Anti-patterns and limits: when instances differ by a whole substance (with many properties), you cannot be certain which property produced the difference; thus strict applicability is often hard to realize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine Agreement and Difference when strict Method of Difference cannot be satisfied; seek multiple instances and counter-instances that collectively isolate a common property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when you cannot find a single instance pair differing only by one circumstance. Strengthen inference by showing many substances that act as antidotes all share a particular property (e.g., forming insoluble compounds) while differing in other properties. This may approach the rigor of the Method of Difference without achieving its maximum certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer causal connection when the degree or direction of variation in one quantity is found to be invariable concomitant with variation in another quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when antecedent and consequent vary continuously or by degrees (e.g., capacity of neighboring body for supporting opposite electricity limits conductor charge; degree of dew deposition varies with radiative/conductive properties). Caution: when observed variations are small relative to possible ranges, very different laws may produce similar numerical results within narrow limits — so extrapolating numerical laws beyond observed extremes is hazardous. Concomitant variation evidence can establish proportional relations but may not prove exclusivity of cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract from a phenomenon the effects that can be attributed to known causes; attribute the remaining (residual) part to some other cause(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not independent of deduction: requires prior knowledge/deduction about what known causes would produce. Use when you can account for part of the phenomenon by known causes and isolate the remainder. The text notes it 'is not independent of deduction' though it requires specific experience and can be included among direct methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary operation: precise definition and delimitation of the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Before investigating causation, define exactly what the phenomenon is and distinguish it from similar phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define 'dew' as 'the spontaneous appearance of moisture on substances exposed in the open air when no rain or visible wet is falling.' This preliminary separation (from rain, fog, etc.) is necessary to assemble valid instances for application of the inductive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour requirement for Method of Difference (only-one-circumstance condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Method of Difference to conclusively identify a cause, the compared instances must agree in every circumstance except the one alleged to be causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that failure to meet this condition weakens inference (e.g., antidotes might differ in many properties). Where perfect conformity is impossible, gather multiple diverse instances to reduce chance of confounding properties; otherwise accept lower certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Concomitant Variations when a quality cannot be excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: When a candidate causal quality is present to differing degrees across instances and cannot be wholly excluded, use concomitant variation to detect proportional relations between degree of quality and amount of effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in the dew example: a 'scale of intensity' appears when varying heat-conducting power, radiative power, and texture. Where a quality continuously varies across materials, concomitant variation is the only practicable method to infer its causal role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive corroboration of inductive inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, deduce the effect from established laws of the agents involved to corroborate inductive conclusions and to explain exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use laws of aqueous vapor and heat to deduce why lowering temperature causes condensation (dew) and why very dry air prevents dew despite cooling. Deduction can both prove causation and account for exceptions that observation-based methods miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental verification and natural experiment as tests of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Corroborate inductive hypotheses by controlled experiments (manipulating antecedents) and by observing natural experiments where a single definite change occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: artificially cooling a surface to produce dew (controlled experiment); withdrawal of clouds creating rapid cooling and subsequent dew deposition (natural experiment). Such tests satisfy Method of Difference requisitions when they introduce a single definite change and show the consequent follows rapidly, reducing chance of confounding changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about extrapolating numerical laws beyond observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that the numerical law of variation observed within narrow limits will hold for much larger or smaller quantities beyond those limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical fact: different laws can yield very similar numerical values within narrow ranges, diverging only over larger ranges. Examples: empirical formulae for elasticity of steam or resistance of fluids failed beyond observation limits. Thus conclusions from concomitant variations may only be secure within the observed extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing cause from effect (directionality of causal inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish whether a correlated antecedent is the cause or the effect (or both effects of a common cause) by gathering additional facts and applying difference/concomitant variation/deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in dew: first find that dewed objects are colder than air (agreement), then show that objects have properties that make them become colder independently of dew (concomitant variations and deduction), thus concluding coldness causes dew rather than the reverse. Use multiple methods to resolve directionality.
